summaries.gardner: Scotiabank is a well-known incumbent in a mature industry, not an emerging-industry leader with a hard-to-copy innovative edge, so it fits Rule Breaker investing poorly. Its strong 2026 share-price momentum (about 40% over 52 weeks) is the main Rule Breaker trait it shows.
summaries.buffett: Scotiabank is an understandable bank with a 190-year record and dividends paid continuously since 1833, the kind of franchise Buffett has owned in banks. But its returns have lagged peers (FY2025 reported ROE 9.7%), reported EPS of C$5.67 in FY2025 was no higher than in FY2015, and at about 2x book there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would see a simple, regulated oligopoly business with low odds of failure, but also a mediocre-return bank whose Latin American expansion consumed capital for a decade without lifting earnings per share. The current turnaround under Scott Thomson improves returns but does not make it a great business at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: Scotiabank fits Lynch's turnaround or stalwart category: adjusted EPS is expected to rise about 20% in FY2026 after restructuring, while the bank pays a 3.5% dividend and buys back stock. At about 15x forward earnings the P/E is below this year's growth, but long-run growth is mid-single-digit, so the bargain depends on the turnaround holding.
summaries.fisher: Fisher looked for companies with long runways and strong research and sales organisations; Scotiabank is a mature bank with modest product innovation and middling customer satisfaction. Management's capital reallocation is rational and candid, but growth prospects fall short of Fisher's standard.
summaries.graham: Scotiabank passes Graham's size, dividend-record and ten-year profitability tests, but fails on earnings growth (reported diluted EPS of C$5.67 in both FY2015 and FY2025) and on price, with a P/E near 17 and price-to-book near 2.0 giving a product of about 34, above his 22.5 ceiling.
summaries.thiel: Scotiabank is a commodity-like universal bank without proprietary technology or a monopoly secret; it competes in an oligopoly rather than having created a new market. It scores poorly on Thiel's seven questions apart from durability and distribution.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours companies riding big platform shifts with disciplined cost structures; Scotiabank has embraced cost discipline (FTEs down to 81,734 from 87,317 in a year) and its earnings are rising, but it is not a beneficiary of AI or cloud as a core growth driver. It fits his 'get fit' discipline more than his growth focus.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating (Q3 2026 adjusted net income up 18% year on year to C$2,973M, adjusted EPS C$2.28), analysts' estimates have been beaten four quarters running and the stock has strong momentum, which suits Druckenmiller's focus on earnings direction. Its sensitivity to interest rates, credit cycles and Latin American macro makes the liquidity backdrop key.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids banks because their returns depend on leverage and they lack high returns on unleveraged capital; Scotiabank's ~10-14% ROE on a balance sheet levered about 16x equity does not meet his test of a good company.
summaries.greenblatt: Greenblatt's Magic Formula excludes banks because return on capital and earnings yield are not meaningful for leveraged lenders. On its own terms, Scotiabank's earnings yield of about 6% on trailing reported EPS is reasonable but not deep value.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a high-return business, skilled and honest management, and reinvestment runway; Scotiabank has capable management and some runway but its returns on equity have been mediocre and depend on leverage. It is a partial fit at best.
summaries.pabrai: Scotiabank is a simple, existing business with low risk of permanent loss, but it is not a distressed bargain: the shares have risen about 40% in a year and trade near analysts' targets. Pabrai's 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup is not clearly present now.
summaries.wood: Scotiabank is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing); it is a traditional incumbent that fintech challengers target. It does not fit Cathie Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and pricing power; Scotiabank is simple and durable but not dominant, and bank cash flows are not readily predictable. Its ongoing turnaround toward a 14%+ ROE is the kind of catalyst he might watch.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale-economics-shared businesses that pass savings to customers; Scotiabank does not compete that way, and its customer satisfaction trails peers. It fits his approach poorly.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine backed young companies attacking huge markets with new technology; a 190-year-old bank is the opposite of that profile, so the framework barely applies.
summaries.nash: Scotiabank passes Nash's screens on scale, a 1.34% short interest, profitability and four straight earnings beats, but fails on revenue growth below 10%, the banker's leverage test and meaningful free cash flow, and has no secular trend tailwind; it scores about 60 of 130 on his 13 categories.

momentum.evidence: BNS's NYSE shares rose about 40% over the 52 weeks to mid-October 2026, to US$91.60 on October 16 from a 52-week low of US$63.68, well ahead of the broad market.

g4.evidence: CEO Scott Thomson has lifted adjusted ROE to 14.2% and Euromoney named Scotiabank Canada's best bank in 2024, but it has no famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate BNS Hold (8 of 14 in September 2026) with an average target of about US$90, close to the price, rather than calling it wildly overvalued.

simple.evidence: Scotiabank is a conventional bank that takes deposits, makes loans, sells wealth products and does capital markets business in Canada and Latin America.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year and has paid dividends continuously since 1833, but reported diluted EPS was C$5.67 in both FY2015 and FY2025.

integrity.evidence: Management sets public medium-term targets and reports against them candidly (FY2025 reported ROE 9.7% vs a 14%+ target), and redeployed capital from Colombia, Costa Rica and Panama to North America, but earlier Latin American acquisitions destroyed value.

b6.evidence: Under Thomson the bank has shrunk non-core Latin American markets rather than empire-building, though the US$2.8B KeyCorp stake is a new bet on US banking.

roic.evidence: FY2025 reported ROE was 9.7% (adjusted 11.8%) on a balance sheet with liabilities about 16x equity, so returns rely on leverage and have trailed RBC and TD.

fcf.evidence: Bank free cash flow is not meaningful; operating cash flow swung from C$15,652M in FY2024 to C$5,407M in FY2025 on balance-sheet flows.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings over the past decade did not raise per-share earnings: reported diluted EPS was C$5.67 in FY2015 and in FY2025, and the US share price rose only about 39% in five years.

safety.evidence: At about 17x trailing reported earnings and 2.0x book value, the shares trade around analysts' average target of about US$90, leaving no meaningful margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 15x FY2026 consensus adjusted EPS of C$8.53 and a 3.5% dividend yield is reasonable for a recovering bank, but no longer cheap after a 40% rally.

mu5.evidence: As a domestic systemically important bank with a 13.1% CET1 ratio and AA-range ratings, Scotiabank has few plausible paths to outright failure; the main risks are credit losses and Latin American macro shocks.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in Canada, Mexico and the US (KeyCorp) at its targeted 14%+ ROE, but historically its reinvestment in Latin America earned below-target returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart in a turnaround: a big dividend-paying bank whose adjusted EPS is expected to grow about 20% in FY2026 after restructuring.

ly3.evidence: A forward P/E of about 15 is below the expected 20% FY2026 adjusted EPS growth, but above the roughly 11% growth expected for FY2027.

runway.evidence: Sales can keep growing with the economy and through Mexico and the US, but in mature markets growth is likely mid-single-digit.

ly7.evidence: The bank bought back 8.6 million shares in Q3 2026 and shares outstanding fell to 1,219M from 1,242M a year earlier, but there is no evidence of significant insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Scotiabank is widely covered by analysts in Canada and the US and is a core holding for dividend investors.

fi2.evidence: It has launched new offerings such as the Scene+ partnership with Shell in 2026 and digital banking through Tangerine, but product innovation is incremental.

fi3.evidence: As a bank it does not report R&D spending separately, so the productivity of its technology investment cannot be measured directly.

fi4.evidence: Its customer satisfaction ranks last among Canada's Big Five (J.D. Power 2025), and its strategy focuses on earning more primary relationships, a sign selling is not a standout strength.

longterm.evidence: Management accepted losses (a C$1,422M impairment and C$434M additional loss) to exit Colombia, Costa Rica and Panama for long-term returns, but it still manages tightly to near-term ROE and EPS targets.

gr1.evidence: Scotiabank had C$1.55 trillion of assets at July 31, 2026 and a market value of about US$112B.

ni10.evidence: It has been profitable every year, with net income ranging from C$6,853M (FY2020) to C$10,174M (FY2022) over FY2016-FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Scotiabank declared its first dividend on July 1, 1833 and has paid continuously since.

eps10.evidence: Reported diluted EPS was C$5.67 in FY2015 and C$5.67 in FY2025; even adjusted FY2025 EPS of C$7.09 is only 25% higher, short of one third.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 17 on reported EPS of about C$7.65 is above Graham's limit of about 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 16.9 times price-to-book of about 2.0 gives about 34, above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: Scotiabank has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; its products are standard banking products.

timing.evidence: Falling credit losses and rising margins are lifting earnings now (Q3 2026 NIM 2.49% vs 2.36%), but Canadian and Mexican trade uncertainty clouds the outlook.

th3.evidence: It did not start by dominating a small niche; it is a broad incumbent across many markets.

team.evidence: Thomson is a capable outside CEO who has hit the 14% ROE target in Q3 2026, but the team is not regarded as world-class versus the best global banks.

th5.evidence: Its 1,984 branches and offices, digital channels and Scene+ loyalty program give strong distribution to more than 20 million clients.

durable.evidence: Canada's regulated oligopoly should protect its position for decades, but fintech and digital challengers could erode deposits and younger clients.

th7.evidence: Scotiabank is not pursuing a unique opportunity others miss; its North American pivot follows peers into the US.

trend.evidence: It is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud; it uses them to cut costs like every other bank.

dr1.evidence: Q3 2026 adjusted net income rose 18% year on year to C$2,973M (adjusted EPS C$2.28) and beat consensus in each of the last four quarters, with FY2026 consensus adjusted EPS of C$8.53 (+20%).

dr2.evidence: Continued cost savings, buybacks and normalising credit costs could lift returns further, but much of the turnaround is already reflected in the 40% share-price rise.

dr4.evidence: Bank of Canada rate cuts help loan demand and credit quality, while trade tensions and slower growth in Canada and Mexico work against it.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the Q4 FY2026 results on December 2, 2026, the Scotia Group Jamaica buyout, ongoing buybacks and possible upside from the KeyCorp and Davivienda stakes.

dr7.evidence: Its middling returns, macro sensitivity and modest growth make it unsuitable for a large, high-conviction position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is not meaningful for a bank; its net margin was 20.6% in FY2025 (25.2% adjusted) and 26.3% in nine-month FY2026.

fcfyield.evidence: Bank free cash flow is not meaningful; the earnings yield of about 5.9% on trailing reported EPS and the 3.5% dividend yield are better gauges.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not a meaningful measure for a bank whose deposits and debt are operating items.

pa2.evidence: Scotiabank went through a fixable setback of weak returns and Latin American restructuring, which is now largely being repaired with ROE back above 14%.

pa4.evidence: With a 13.1% CET1 ratio, AA-range ratings and Canada's oligopoly, the risk of permanent loss is low even if earnings fluctuate.

wo1.evidence: Scotiabank is a traditional bank, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Banking costs do not fall sharply with volume in a way that opens large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market grows with the economies of Canada, Mexico and the US, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its earnings are sensitive to interest rates, credit cycles, currency moves and commodity-linked economies such as Chile and Peru.

ns1.evidence: It does not systematically pass scale savings to customers; it prices in line with Big Five peers.

ns4.evidence: Its position should be somewhat stronger as its North American pivot matures, but not clearly so given digital competition.

va2.evidence: Banking solves important needs (safe savings, mortgages, credit), but Scotiabank's offer is not uniquely better than rivals'.

tn1.evidence: Scotiabank is an established bank, not a company built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market still sees a Latin America-heavy bank while it is becoming more North American (KeyCorp stake, Mexico, exit from Colombia and Central America), though the shift is gradual.

tn3.evidence: It is a US$112B large-cap Canadian bank, outside Nash's zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable and revenue has grown since FY2021 (C$31,252M to C$37,741M in FY2025); as a bank it carries more liabilities than cash, a structural feature of lending.

tn5.evidence: Quarterly free cash flow and cash-versus-debt are not meaningful for a bank whose cash flows swing with deposits and trading.

tn6.evidence: Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 7.4% to C$30,018M and FY2026 consensus growth is about 7.6%, below 10%.

tn7.evidence: Free-cash-flow margin is not meaningful for a bank, so the Rule of 40 cannot be applied.

tn8.evidence: Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 7.4% while adjusted non-interest expenses rose 4.7% (reported expenses fell 3.9%).

tn9.evidence: BNS trips the revenue-growth kill (7.4% nine-month growth) and, as a bank, its liabilities far exceed its cash.

tn10.evidence: There is no major legal threat comparable to TD's AML case, but it operates under heavy regulation in many countries and faces political and trade risk in Mexico and Latin America.

tn11.evidence: Scotiabank provides deposits, loans, cards and investment services that help households and businesses in Canada and Latin America save, borrow and grow, and charges interest spreads and fees.

tn13.evidence: Total about 60: cash vs debt 5, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue dipped in FY2021, pre-tax margin fell from 41.0% in FY2021 to 27.8% in FY2025, and free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank.

tn15.evidence: As a bank, Scotiabank's total liabilities of C$1,457,645M are about 16.1x its C$90,622M of equity (July 31, 2026), far above the 4x test.

tn18.evidence: Thomson has delivered higher ROE and record quarterly profit since becoming CEO in February 2023, but he has led the bank for under four years and is not a founder; open-market share purchases are not documented.

tn20.evidence: Adjusted EPS beat consensus in each of the last four quarters: C$1.93 vs C$1.84 (Q4 2025), C$2.05 vs C$1.95 (Q1 2026), C$2.02 vs C$1.93 (Q2 2026) and C$2.28 vs C$2.10 (Q3 2026).

tn21.evidence: There is no co-CEO, auditor issue or accounting suspicion, but pre-tax margins declined over five years and the bank has taken large impairments on past Latin American deals.

tn22.evidence: Scotiabank has substantial revenue (C$37,741M in FY2025), steady profits and buys back rather than issues shares, so it avoids the hype trap.

tn24.evidence: At about 15x forward earnings with a 3.5% yield, the price implies mid-single-digit growth, below the 20% FY2026 adjusted EPS rebound but close to its 7%+ medium-term EPS target.

tn25.evidence: Nash's free-cash-flow DCF cannot be applied meaningfully to a bank, whose reported free cash flow is driven by balance-sheet flows.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 15.2 against 20% expected FY2026 adjusted EPS growth gives a PEG of about 0.75, but on FY2027 growth of about 11% the PEG is about 1.2, roughly in line with Canadian bank peers.
